summary: Suggests a pair of TCP options for using alternate data checksum algorithms in the TCP header, and corrects errors introduced in editing RFC 1145. It is experimental and not for production. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1146 describes experimental TCP options for choosing an alternate checksum during connection setup and carrying longer checksum values. Both endpoints must name the same algorithm or use the standard TCP checksum; RFC 6247 later obsoleted this memo.

questions: what are tcp alternate checksum options
subtitle: Experimental TCP options for negotiating an alternate checksum algorithm.

tldr.problem: Some systems wanted checksum algorithms with different error-detection properties from the standard TCP checksum.
tldr.mechanism: A request option in SYN segments negotiates an algorithm; a data option carries checksum bytes when the result is longer than the TCP header's checksum field.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1146 is Historic, obsoleted by RFC 6247, and itself obsoletes RFC 1145. The memo says the options are experimental and not recommended for production use.

today: RFC 1146 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6247. It obsoletes RFC 1145.

sections.title: Requesting an Alternate Checksum
sections.content:
The memo defines a TCP Alternate Checksum Request Option that a TCP may send in a SYN segment to indicate it can generate and receive checksums using an alternate algorithm. The option has Kind 14, Length 3, and an algorithm number.

If both SYN segments carry the option and name the same algorithm, the connection uses it after the SYN segments. If either side omits the option or the values differ, the connection uses the standard TCP checksum. SYN and RST segments always use the standard checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint can request a checksum algorithm during connection setup. The endpoints use it only if both request the same one; otherwise, they keep the standard checksum.

sections.title: Carrying a Longer Checksum
sections.content:
The TCP Alternate Checksum Data Option has Kind 15 and carries extra checksum bytes when the negotiated algorithm produces more than 16 bits. Depending on the checksum, the value may be split between the TCP checksum field and the option, or placed entirely in the option.

The data option is not used with a 16-bit checksum algorithm. An otherwise acceptable segment with an inappropriate option or byte count must be discarded, a reset segment generated, and the connection aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: When an alternate checksum is longer than 16 bits, the data option carries the extra bytes. A segment with an option that does not fit the chosen algorithm is rejected.

sections.title: Defined Algorithms and Status
sections.content:
Algorithm value 0 selects the standard TCP checksum. Value 1 selects the 8-bit Fletcher algorithm, which produces a 16-bit checksum. Value 2 selects the 16-bit Fletcher algorithm, which produces a 32-bit checksum. The RFC notes that the Fletcher algorithms can detect transposition of octets or words within a datagram.

The memo says the options are experimental and not recommended for production use. It corrects errors introduced while editing RFC 1145.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo defines the standard checksum and two Fletcher alternatives. It is an experimental proposal and does not recommend production use.
